Base Converter

Place ValueArithmeticNumber Theory
Game: Four boxes show one number written in four different counting systems, such as binary. There is nothing to win — just explore.
How to play: Type a number in a box and press Enter, or press Convert. Use the plus and minus buttons to change a box's counting system.
Look for the math

A number is not the same thing as the digits we write for it. One amount can be written in many ways, and this device shows four of them side by side.

Places are worth powers

In ordinary base ten, 365 means 3 hundreds, 6 tens and 5 ones. In any positional system each place is worth a power of the base: in base two the places are ones, twos, fours, eights and so on. The number does not move when you change its base — only its name does. That is why the converter can fill all four boxes from one entry.

Digits up to Z

After the digits 0 to 9 we use the letters A to Z, so the largest digit in base sixteen is F and the largest in base thirty-six is Z. The applet prints capital letters, and so does this page. For example 10 in binary is two, and FF in hexadecimal is 255. The four bases start at 10, 2, 8 and 16, and each one can be set to any whole number from 2 to 36.

Fractions that do not end

The part after the dot is counted the same way, with each place worth a fraction of the one before. Some fractions stop: half is 0.1 in binary. Some never stop, like a third in base ten. The original applet worked these out with ordinary double-precision numbers and stopped after 36 digits, adding ... for a tail that had not ended. This port does the same, so what you see matches the applet digit for digit. One small quirk comes from the original: a negative fraction smaller than one, such as -0.5, loses its minus sign, because the applet reads the whole part from -0.

What was checked

The page says the bases run from 2 to 36, that negative numbers and fractions are accepted, and that four bases are shown at once. All three are true. The logic test tries every one of the 35 input bases against every one of the 35 output bases (1,225 pairs), checks negatives and fractions, and compares every answer with a second transcription of the applet's own method. One small difference: the page says the number appears in the three remaining boxes, but the applet also rewrites the box you typed in, tidying it into capital digits; this port follows the applet.

Type 0.1 in the base-3 box and watch what appears in base 10. Then try -0.5 and see the quirk for yourself.
